===Development in Gandhara (3rd century BCE–5th century CE)=== [[File:ButkaraStupa.jpg|thumb|Butkara Stupa in Gandhara]] [[File:Ahin Posh stupa reconstitution, Simpson 1878.jpg|thumb|The {{ill|Ahin Posh|en|Ahin Posh|WD=Q4695118|lt=Ahin Posh|1=Ahin Posh}} stupa was dedicated in the 2nd century CE under the [[:en:Kushans|Kushans]] and contained coins of [[:en:Kaniska I|Kaniska I]].]] [[File:Restored_view_of_the_Manikyala_Stupa.jpg|thumb|{{ill|Manikyala Stupa|en|Manikyala Stupa|WD=Q25379332|lt=Manikyala Stupa|1=Manikyala Stupa}}, from the period of [[:en:Kaniska I|Kaniska I]]]]
The stupa underwent major evolutions in the area of Gandhara. Since Buddhism spread to {{ill|Central Asia|en|Central Asia|WD=Q27275|lt=Central Asia|1=Central Asia}}, China, and ultimately Korea and Japan through Gandhara, the stylistic evolution of the Gandharan stupa was very influential in the later development of the stupa (and related artistic or [[:en:Architectural form|Architectural form]]s) in these areas.{{sfnp|Le|2010|p=181}} The Gandhara stupa followed several steps, generally moving towards more and more elevation and addition of decorative elements, leading eventually to the development of the {{ill|Pagoda|en|Pagoda|WD=Q199451|lt=Pagoda|1=Pagoda}} tower.{{sfnp|Le|2010|pp=182–183}} The main stupa types are, in chronological order:
# The {{ill|Dharmarajika Stupa|en|Dharmarajika Stupa|WD=Q5269314|lt=Dharmarajika Stupa|1=Dharmarajika Stupa}}, with a near-Indian design of a semi-hemispheric stupa almost directly on the ground surface, probably dated to the 3rd century BCE. Similar stupas are the {{ill|Butkara Stupa|en|Butkara Stupa|WD=Q5002535|lt=Butkara Stupa|1=Butkara Stupa}}, the [[:en:Manikyala|Manikyala]] stupa, or the Chakpat stupa.{{sfnp|Le|2010|p=173}} # The {{ill|Saidu Sharif Stupa|en|Saidu Sharif Stupa|WD=Q40795218|lt=Saidu Sharif Stupa|1=Saidu Sharif Stupa}}, pillared and [[:en:Quincunxial|Quincunxial]], with a flight of stairs to a dome elevated on a square platform. Many Gandhara miniatures represent this type (1st century CE).{{sfnp|Le|2010|pp=174–176}} # The {{ill|Loriyan Tangai|en|Loriyan Tangai|WD=Q52791921|lt=Loriyan Tangai|1=Loriyan Tangai}} stupa, with an elongated shape and many narrative reliefs, in many ways the classic Gandharan stupa (2nd century CE).{{sfnp|Le|2010|pp=176–177}} # The near-pyramidal {{ill|Jaulian|en|Jaulian|WD=Q593411|lt=Jaulian|1=Jaulian}} stupa (2nd century CE).{{sfnp|Le|2010|p=179}} # The {{ill|Cruciform|en|Cruciform|WD=Q5189819|lt=Cruciform|1=Cruciform}} type, as in the {{ill|Bhamala Stupa|en|Bhamala Stupa|WD=Q18110458|lt=Bhamala Stupa|1=Bhamala Stupa}}, with flights of stairs in the four cardinal directions (4th century CE).{{sfnp|Le|2010|p=178}} # The towering design of the second {{ill|Kanishka Stupa|en|Kanishka Stupa|WD=Q842918|lt=Kanishka Stupa|1=Kanishka Stupa}} (4th–5th century CE).<ref name=BA>{{harvp|Le|2010|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=9jb364g4BvoC&pg=PA179 179–180]}}.</ref>
<gallery widths="150px" heights="150px"> StupaWithPillarsGandhara2ndCentury.jpg|A model resembling the {{ill|Saidu Sharif Stupa|en|Saidu Sharif Stupa|WD=Q40795218|lt=Saidu Sharif Stupa|1=Saidu Sharif Stupa}}, with square base and four columns (1st century CE).{{sfnp|Le|2010|pp=174–176}} Loriyan Tangai complete Stupa.jpg|{{ill|Loriyan Tangai|en|Loriyan Tangai|WD=Q52791921|lt=Loriyan Tangai|1=Loriyan Tangai}} decorated stupa, in the {{ill|Greco-Buddhist art|en|Greco-Buddhist art|WD=Q1008014|lt=Greco-Buddhist art|1=Greco-Buddhist art}} of Gandhara (2nd century CE). Jaulian Stupa A11 reliquary.jpg|A tower-shaped stupa, thought to be the design of the second (rebuilt) {{ill|Kanishka Stupa|en|Kanishka Stupa|WD=Q842918|lt=Kanishka Stupa|1=Kanishka Stupa}}, {{ill|Jaulian|en|Jaulian|WD=Q593411|lt=Jaulian|1=Jaulian}} monastery<ref name=BA/> Stupa Reliquary Kushan period, about 2nd century CE.jpg|Stupa-shaped reliquary, {{ill|Kushan Empire|en|Kushan Empire|WD=Q25979|lt=Kushan|1=Kushan Empire}} period, about 2nd century CE Chilas petroglyphs, Buddhist stupa circa 300-350 CE.jpg|{{ill|Chilas|en|Chilas|WD=Q2414959|lt=Chilas|1=Chilas}} petroglyphs, Buddhist stupa, {{circa|300–350}} CE based on paleography<ref>Dated "between A.D. 300–350 based on Kharosthi, Brahmi, and Sodian inscriptions written before and after the drawing was completed (fig. 3). In the center of the triptych, a spectacular stupa with a relatively small dome [anda], a chattravali with seven disks, columns, banners, and multiple bells illustrates a trend towards decorative profusion." {{cite journal |journal=Bulletin of the Asia Institute |date=2002 |title=Chital petroglyphs|page=152 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RuhtAAAAMAAJ&pg=PA152 |publisher=Wayne State University Press}}</ref> </gallery>
====Origin of the pyramidal temple==== {{multiple image|total_width=400 | header=Pyramidal temples | align = right | caption_align = center | image1 = Kumrahar Mahabodhi plaque.jpg | caption1 = The Mahabodhi Temple in 150–200 CE | image2 = Top of Temple.jpg | caption2 = The {{ill|Mahabodhi Temple|en|Mahabodhi Temple|WD=Q4513|lt=Mahabodhi Temple|1=Mahabodhi Temple}}: a stepped pyramid with round stupa on top<ref name=BA238/> | image3=India, Bihar, 10th century - Model of the Sikhara of a Buddhist Temple - 1971.167 - Cleveland Museum of Art.tif | caption3= Model of the [[:en:Sikhara|Sikhara]] of a Buddhist temple; 900s }}
It is thought that the temple in the shape of a truncated pyramid may have derived from the design of the stepped stupas that developed in Gandhara. The {{ill|Mahabodhi Temple|en|Mahabodhi Temple|WD=Q4513|lt=Mahabodhi Temple|1=Mahabodhi Temple}} in Bodh Gaya is one such example, formed of a succession of steps with niches containing Buddha images, alternating with Greco-Roman pillars.<ref name=BA238>{{harvp|Le|2010|pp=238–248}}.</ref> The structure is crowned by the shape of a hemispherical stupa topped by {{ill|Finial|en|Finial|WD=Q1406758|lt=Finial|1=Finial}}s, forming a logical elongation of the stepped Gandharan stupas such as those seen in {{ill|Jaulian|en|Jaulian|WD=Q593411|lt=Jaulian|1=Jaulian}}.<ref name=BA238/>
Although the current structure of the Mahabdhodi Temple dates to the {{ill|Gupta Empire|en|Gupta Empire|WD=Q11774|lt=Gupta|1=Gupta Empire}} period (5th century CE), the "Plaque of Mahabhodi Temple", discovered in [[:en:Kumrahar|Kumrahar]] and dated to 150–200 CE, based on its dated [[:en:Kharoshthi|Kharoshthi]] inscriptions and combined finds of {{ill|Huvishka|en|Huvishka|WD=Q1396420|lt=Huvishka|1=Huvishka}} coins, suggests that the pyramidal structure already existed in the 2nd century CE.<ref name=BA238/> This is confirmed by archaeological excavations in Bodh Gaya.<ref name=BA238/>
This truncated pyramid design also marked the evolution from the [[:en:Aniconic|Aniconic]] stupa dedicated to the cult of relics, to the {{ill|Cultural icon|en|Cultural icon|WD=Q3139104|lt=iconic|1=Cultural icon}} temple with multiple images of the Buddha and Bodhisattvas.<ref name=BA238/> This design was influential in the development of later {{ill|Hindu temple|en|Hindu temple|WD=Q842402|lt=Hindu temple|1=Hindu temple}}s.{{sfnp|Le|2010|p=234}}
===Expansion in Asia=== ====Asian stupas==== (523 CE) is thought to derive from the Gandharan tower-stupa model.{{sfnp|Le|2010|p=180}}]] [[File:Row of stupas on roadside east of Leh, Ladakh.jpg|thumb|Row of [[:en:Chorten|Chorten]] stupas on roadside east of Leh, Ladakh]]
Stupa architecture was adopted in {{ill|Southeast Asia|en|Southeast Asia|WD=Q11708|lt=Southeast|1=Southeast Asia}} and {{ill|East Asia|en|East Asia|WD=Q27231|lt=East Asia|1=East Asia}}, where it became prominent as a Buddhist monument used for enshrining sacred relics.<ref name=Ency/> The Indian gateway arches, ''torana'', reached East Asia with the spread of Buddhism.<ref>Encyclopædia Britannica (2008), ''torii''</ref> Some scholars hold that ''[[torii]]'' derives from the torana gates at the Buddhist historic site of Sanchi (3rd century BCE–11th century CE).<ref name=Jaanus>[http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/ Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System (2001), ''torii''.]</ref> In {{ill|Tibet|en|Tibet|WD=Q17252|lt=Tibet|1=Tibet}}, the stupa became the chorten,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bhutanmajestictravel.com/buddhism/stupa|access-date=17 January 2013|title=Stupa – Bhutanese, Nepalese, Tibetan Style Chortens or Stupa is the symbol of enlightened mind|publisher=Bhutan Majestic Travel|date=17 January 2013|url-status = dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121231185528/http://www.bhutanmajestictravel.com/buddhism/stupa|archive-date=31 December 2012}}</ref> and the pagoda in East Asia.<ref>''The Columbia Encyclopedia'', 6th ed., Columbia University Press{{page?|date=July 2024}}</ref> The pagoda has varied forms that also include bell-shaped and pyramidal styles. In the Western context, there is no clear distinction between a stupa and a pagoda. In general, however, "stupa" is the term used for a Buddhist structure in India or Southeast Asia, while "pagoda" refers to a building in East Asia that can be entered and that may be used for secular purposes. However, use of the term varies by region. For example, stupas in Burma tend to be referred to as "pagodas".
Stupas were built in {{ill|Sri Lanka|en|Sri Lanka|WD=Q854|lt=Sri Lanka|1=Sri Lanka}} soon after [[:en:Devanampiya Tissa of Anuradhapura|Devanampiya Tissa of Anuradhapura]] converted to Buddhism. The first was the {{ill|Thuparamaya|en|Thuparamaya|WD=Q7799227|lt=Thuparamaya|1=Thuparamaya}}. Later, many more were built over the years, including the {{ill|Jetavanaramaya|en|Jetavanaramaya|WD=Q1961579|lt=Jetavanaramaya|1=Jetavanaramaya}} in Anuradhapura.
====Development of the pagoda==== The Asian words for pagoda (''tā'' in Chinese, ''t'ap'' in Korean, ''tháp'' in Vietnamese, ''tō'' in Japanese) are all thought to derive from the {{ill|Pali|en|Pali|WD=Q36727|lt=Pali|1=Pali}} word for stupa, ''thupa'', with the {{ill|Sanskrit|en|Sanskrit|WD=Q11059|lt=Sanskrit|1=Sanskrit}} pronunciation being ''stupa''.{{sfnp|Le|2010|p=183}} In particular the type of the tower-like stupa, the last stage of Gandharan stupa development, visible in the second {{ill|Kanishka Stupa|en|Kanishka Stupa|WD=Q842918|lt=Kanishka Stupa|1=Kanishka Stupa}} (4th century), is thought to be the precursor of the tower stupas in {{ill|Turkestan|en|Turkestan|WD=Q1315785|lt=Turkestan|1=Turkestan}} and the Chinese pagodas such as {{ill|Songyue Pagoda|en|Songyue Pagoda|WD=Q2046262|lt=Songyue Pagoda|1=Songyue Pagoda}} (523 CE).{{sfnp|Le|2010|p=180}}
==Notable stupas== [[File:Borobudur temple panorama.jpg|thumb|{{ill|Borobudur|en|Borobudur|WD=Q42798|lt=Borobudur|1=Borobudur}} bell-shaped stupas]]
The earliest archaeological evidence for the presence of Buddhist stupas dates to the late 4th century BCE. Some of the oldest known examples of stupas are found in Vaishali, Kushinagar, Piprahwa, Ramgram, Sanchi, {{ill|Sarnath|en|Sarnath|WD=Q324394|lt=Sarnath|1=Sarnath}}, Amaravati, and Bharhut.
With the top of its spire reaching {{convert|120.45|m|ft|abbr=on}} in height, {{ill|Phra Pathommachedi|en|Phra Pathommachedi|WD=Q1150964|lt=Phra Pathommachedi|1=Phra Pathommachedi}} in Nakhon Pathom, Thailand is the tallest extant stupa in the world.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.jedeethai.com/เจดีย์พระธาตุภาคกลาง/พระปฐมเจดีย์.html|title=พระปฐมเจดีย์|website= jedeethai.com}}</ref> The {{ill|Swat River|en|Swat River|WD=Q2372276|lt=Swat Valley|1=Swat River}} hosts a well-preserved stupa at Shingardar near {{ill|Ghalegay|en|Ghalegay|WD=Q13139680|lt=Ghalegay|1=Ghalegay}}; another stupa is located near {{ill|Barikot|en|Barikot|WD=Q3634988|lt=Barikot|1=Barikot}} and Dharmarajika-Taxila in Pakistan. In Sri Lanka, the ancient city of {{ill|Anuradhapura|en|Anuradhapura|WD=Q5724|lt=Anuradhapura|1=Anuradhapura}} includes some of the tallest, most ancient, and best-preserved stupas in the world, such as {{ill|Ruwanwelisaya|en|Ruwanwelisaya|WD=Q3534755|lt=Ruwanwelisaya|1=Ruwanwelisaya}}.
The most elaborate stupa is the 8th-century {{ill|Borobudur|en|Borobudur|WD=Q42798|lt=Borobudur|1=Borobudur}} monument in Java, Indonesia. The upper rounded terrace, with rows of bell-shaped stupas, contain Buddha images symbolizing {{ill|Dhyana in Buddhism|en|Dhyana in Buddhism|WD=Q6577829|lt=Arūpajhāna|1=Dhyana in Buddhism}}, the sphere of formlessness. The main stupa itself is empty, symbolizing complete perfection of enlightenment. The main stupa is the crown part of the monument, while the base is a pyramidal structure elaborated with galleries adorned with [[:en:Bas-relief|Bas-relief]] scenes derived from Buddhist texts and depicting the life of {{ill|The Buddha|en|The Buddha|WD=Q9441|lt=Gautama Buddha|1=The Buddha}}. Borobudur's unique and significant architecture has been acknowledged by {{ill|UNESCO|en|UNESCO|WD=Q7809|lt=UNESCO|1=UNESCO}} as the largest Buddhist monument in the world. It is also the world's largest Buddhist temple<ref name="Guiness"> {{cite web| url=http://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/records-3000/largest-buddhist-temple/| title=Largest Buddhist temple| publisher=Guinness World Records| work=[[Guinness World Records]]| access-date=27 January 2014}}</ref><ref name="JakartaPost1"> {{cite web|url = http://www.thejakartapost.com/news/2012/07/04/guinness-names-borobudur-world-s-largest-buddha-temple.html|title = Guinness names Borobudur world's largest Buddha temple|author = Purnomo Siswoprasetjo|date = 4 July 2012 |publisher = The Jakarta Post|access-date = 27 January 2014|url-status = dead|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20141105191424/http://www.thejakartapost.com/news/2012/07/04/guinness-names-borobudur-world-s-largest-buddha-temple.html|archive-date = 5 November 2014}}</ref> as well as one of the greatest Buddhist monuments in the world.<ref name="unesco-whc">{{cite web| url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/592| title=Borobudur Temple Compounds| publisher={{ill|UNESCO|en|UNESCO|WD=Q7809|lt=UNESCO|1=UNESCO}}| work=[[UNESCO World Heritage Centre]]| access-date=28 December 2008}}</ref>
[[File:Holi_relief,_Mathura,_c1st_century_CE.jpg|thumb|A {{ill|Jain stupa|en|Jain stupa|WD=Q85770537|lt=Jain stupa|1=Jain stupa}}, {{ill|Mathura|en|Mathura|WD=Q200311|lt=Mathura|1=Mathura}}, 1st century CE]]
A {{ill|Jain stupa|en|Jain stupa|WD=Q85770537|lt=Jain stupa|1=Jain stupa}} was excavated at {{ill|Mathura|en|Mathura|WD=Q200311|lt=Mathura|1=Mathura}} in the 19th century.{{sfnp|Smith|1901}}
The {{ill|Shwedagon Pagoda|en|Shwedagon Pagoda|WD=Q464535|lt=Shwedagon Pagoda|1=Shwedagon Pagoda}} in Yangon, Myanmar, is one of the largest stupas in the world.
===European stupas=== {{See also|Buddhism in Europe}}
The {{ill|Benalmádena Stupa|en|Benalmádena Stupa|WD=Q1817748|lt=Benalmádena Stupa|1=Benalmádena Stupa}} is the tallest stupa in Europe. It is {{convert|33|m|ft|abbr=on}} high and was inaugurated on 5 October 2003, the final project of Buddhist master [[:en:Lopon Tsechu Rinpoche|Lopon Tsechu Rinpoche]]. Lopon Tsechu built his first stupa at [[Kalachakra stupa#Stupa in Karma Guen, Spain, 1994|Karma Guen]] near Málaga, in 1994,<ref>[http://www.karmaguen.org/ Karma Guen]</ref> a symbol of peace and prosperity for Spain.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.andalucia.com/benalmadena/benalmadena-pueblo/buddhist-temple|title=Buddhist Stupa|date=27 February 2013}}</ref> He went on to build 16 more stupas in Europe before his death in 2003.
A stupa was built on the ground of the Kalachakra Kalapa Centre in southwest {{ill|Styria|en|Styria|WD=Q41358|lt=Styria|1=Styria}}, Austria, between 2000 and 2002.
A stupa based on the bell-shaped stupas at Borobudur is located at {{ill|Amaravati Buddhist Monastery|en|Amaravati Buddhist Monastery|WD=Q454953|lt=Amaravati Buddhist Monastery|1=Amaravati Buddhist Monastery}}, near {{ill|Hemel Hempstead|en|Hemel Hempstead|WD=Q3532|lt=Hemel Hempstead|1=Hemel Hempstead}}, in the UK.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.buddhamind.info/leftside/arty/progress/stupas.htm|title=Stupa construction at Amaravati Buddhist Monastery|last=friends|first=Venerable Kusalo Bhikkhu – with help from his teachers and|website=www.buddhamind.info|access-date=25 November 2018}}</ref>
===Types of stupas=== [[File:Boudha Stupa 2018 04.jpg|thumb|[[:en:Boudhanath Stupa|Boudhanath Stupa]], Kathmandu, Nepal]]
Built for a variety of reasons, Buddhist stupas are classified, based on form and function, into five types:<ref name="Phuoc2010">{{cite book|author=Le Huu Phuoc|title=Buddhist Architecture|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9jb364g4BvoC&pg=PA140|access-date=8 December 2011|date= 2010|publisher=Grafikol|isbn=978-0-9844043-0-8|page=140}}</ref> * '''Relic stupa''', in which the relics or remains of the Buddha, his disciples, and lay saints are interred * '''Object stupa''', in which the items interred are objects that belonged to the Buddha or his disciples, such as a begging bowls or robes, or important Buddhist scriptures. * '''Commemorative stupa''', built to commemorate events in the lives of Buddha or his disciples * '''Symbolic stupa''', to symbolise aspects of Buddhist theology. For example, Borobudur is considered to be the symbol of "the Three Worlds (''dhatu'') and the spiritual stages (''bhumi'') in a Mahayana ''bodhisattva's'' character".<ref name="Phuoc2010"/> * '''Votive stupa''', constructed to commemorate visits or to gain spiritual benefits, usually at the site of prominent stupas that are regularly visited.
==Symbolism== [[File:Grand Palace Bangkok.jpg|thumb|View of the {{ill|Wat Phra Kaew|en|Wat Phra Kaew|WD=Q1045876|lt=Wat Phra Kaew|1=Wat Phra Kaew}} complex from the northeast]]
"The shape of the stupa represents the Buddha, crowned and sitting in meditation posture on a lion throne. His crown is the top of the spire; his head is the square at the spire's base; his body is the vase shape; his legs are the four steps of the lower terrace; and the base is his throne."<ref name="SINTRO">{{cite web | title=Introduction to stupas | url=http://www.stupa.org.nz/stupa/intro.htm | publisher=stupa.org | access-date=18 April 2009}}</ref>
===Five purified elements=== Although not described in any Tibetan text on stupa symbolism, the stupa may represent the five purified elements, according to Buddhism:<ref name="Beer"/> * The square base represents Earth. * The hemispherical dome/vase represents water. * The conical spire represents fire. * The upper lotus parasol and the crescent moon represent air. * The sun and the dissolving point represent wisdom.
==Construction== To build a stupa, [[Dharma transmission]] and ceremonies known to a {{ill|en:Lama|en|en:Lama|WD=Q191421|lt=Buddhist teacher|1=Lama}} are necessary.<ref name="KUC"/> The type of stupa to be constructed in a certain area is decided together with the teacher assisting in the construction. Sometimes the type chosen is directly connected with events that have taken place in the area.<ref name="KUC">{{cite web | title=Miracle Stupa | url=http://www.stupa.pl/en_stupa.html | publisher=stupa.pl | access-date=18 April 2009}}</ref>
[[Image:EndAscetism.JPG|thumb|The sharing of the relics of the Buddha. {{ill|Greco-Buddhist art|en|Greco-Buddhist art|WD=Q1008014|lt=Greco-Buddhist art|1=Greco-Buddhist art}} of {{ill|Gandhara|en|Gandhara|WD=Q213651|lt=Gandhara|1=Gandhara}}, 2nd–3rd century CE. [[:en:ZenYouMitsu Temple|ZenYouMitsu Temple]] Museum, Tokyo.]] [[Image:Buddha relics.JPG|thumb|Buddha relics from the {{ill|Kanishka Stupa|en|Kanishka Stupa|WD=Q842918|lt=Kanishka Stupa|1=Kanishka Stupa}} in Peshawar, Pakistan. These surviving relics are now housed in [[Mandalay]], Myanmar.]]
===Treasury=== All stupas contain a treasury filled with various objects. Small clay votive offerings called ''tsatsa''s in Tibetan fill most of the treasury. The creation of the ''tsatsa''s is itself a ceremony. Mantras written on paper are made into thin rolls and put into small clay stupas.<ref name="KUC"/> One layer of ''tsatsa''s is placed in the treasury, and the empty space between them is filled with dry sand. On the thus-created new surface, another layer of ''tsatsa''s is made, and so on, until the entire space of the treasury is full.<ref name="KUC"/>
The number of ''tsatsa''s required to completely fill the treasury depends on its size and the size of the ''tsats''a. For example, the {{ill|Kalachakra stupa|en|Kalachakra stupa|WD=Q1103381|lt=Kalachakra stupa|1=Kalachakra stupa}} in southern Spain contains approximately 14,000 ''tsatsa''s.<ref name="KUC"/>
Jewellery and other "precious" objects are also placed in the treasury. It is not necessary that they be expensive, since it is the symbolic value that is important, not the market price.<ref name="KUC"/> It is believed that the more objects are placed in the stupa, the stronger its energy.<ref name="KUC"/>
===Tree of Life=== An important element in every stupa is the "[[:en:Tree of Life|Tree of Life]]". This is a wooden pole covered with gems and thousands of mantras; it is placed in the central channel of the stupa.<ref name="KUC"/> It is positioned during a ceremony or initiation, where the participants hold colorful ribbons connected to the Tree of Life. Together, the participants make their most positive and powerful wishes, which are stored in the Tree of Life. In this way, the stupa is charged and starts to function.<ref name="KUC"/>
===Benefits=== Building a stupa is considered extremely beneficial, leaving very positive {{ill|Karma in Buddhism|en|Karma in Buddhism|WD=Q2673416|lt=karmic|1=Karma in Buddhism}} imprints in the mind. Future benefits from this action are said to result in fortunate rebirths. Fortunate worldly benefits also result, such as being born into a rich family, having a beautiful body, a nice voice, bringing joy to others, and having a long and happy life in which one's wishes are quickly fulfilled.<ref name="SBEN">{{cite web | title=Benefits Resulting from the Building of Stupas | url=http://www.stupa.org.nz/stupa/benefit.htm | publisher=stupa.org | access-date=18 April 2009}}</ref> On the absolute level, one will also be able to quickly reach {{ill|Enlightenment in Buddhism|en|Enlightenment in Buddhism|WD=Q1137019|lt=enlightenment|1=Enlightenment in Buddhism}}, the goal of Buddhism.<ref name="SBEN"/>
Destroying a stupa, on the other hand, is considered an extremely negative deed, similar to murder.<ref name="LTR4">Article: Lopon Tsechu Rinpoche: "The Four Thoughts which Turn the Mind from Samsara." ''Buddhism Today'', Vol. 5, 1998. [http://www.diamondway-teachings.org/export/en/content/advanced/tsechu_4thougths.html Available online] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090303093029/http://www.diamondway-teachings.org/export/en/content/advanced/tsechu_4thougths.html |date=3 March 2009 }}</ref> Such an action is said to create massive negative karmic imprints, leading to serious future problems. It is said this action leaves the mind in a state of paranoia after death has occurred, leading to unfortunate rebirths.<ref name="LTR4"/>
==Tibetan stupas== [[File:Eight great stupas.svg|thumb|left|The Eight Great Stupas]] [[File:Row of chortens at roadside near Kaza, Lahul & Spiti.jpg|thumb|Row of chortens at roadside near {{ill|Leh|en|Leh|WD=Q230818|lt=Leh|1=Leh}}, Ladakh]]
Stupas in {{ill|Tibet|en|Tibet|WD=Q17252|lt=Tibet|1=Tibet}} and Tibetan-influenced regions of the {{ill|Himalayas|en|Himalayas|WD=Q5451|lt=Himalayas|1=Himalayas}}, such as {{ill|Bhutan|en|Bhutan|WD=Q917|lt=Bhutan|1=Bhutan}}, are usually called "chorten" in English, reflecting the term in the {{ill|Tibetic languages|en|Tibetic languages|WD=Q1641150|lt=Tibetan language|1=Tibetic languages}}. There are eight different shapes of chortens in {{ill|Tibetan Buddhism|en|Tibetan Buddhism|WD=Q483889|lt=Tibetan Buddhism|1=Tibetan Buddhism}}, each referring to a major event in the Buddha's life.<ref name="Beer"/> Chortens are often made as a set, placed in a row. The Tibetan set differs slightly (by two events) from the Indian {{ill|The Eight Great Events in the Life of Buddha|en|The Eight Great Events in the Life of Buddha|WD=Q113071555|lt=set of Eight Great Events in the Life of Buddha|1=The Eight Great Events in the Life of Buddha}}.
===Lotus Blossom Stupa=== Also known as "Stupa of Heaped Lotuses", or "Birth of the Sugata Stupa", this stupa refers to the birth of Gautama Buddha. "At birth Buddha took seven steps in each of the four directions"<ref name="Beer">Beer, Robert: ''The Encyclopedia of Tibetan Symbols and Motifs'' (2004) Serindia Publications Inc. {{ISBN|1-932476-10-5}}</ref> (east, south, west, and north). In each direction, lotuses sprang up, symbolizing the {{ill|Brahmavihara|en|Brahmavihara|WD=Q897336|lt=Brahmavihara|1=Brahmavihara}}s: love, compassion, joy, and equanimity. The base of this stupa is circular and has four steps, and it is decorated with lotus-petal designs. Occasionally, seven heaped lotus steps are constructed. These refer to the seven first steps of the Buddha.<ref name="Beer"/>
===Enlightenment Stupa=== [[File:Ogoy Stupa 1 1600x1200.JPG|thumb|left|Enlightenment Stupa at {{ill|Ogoy Island|en|Ogoy Island|WD=Q21044936|lt=Ogoy Island|1=Ogoy Island}}, Russia]]
Also known as the "Stupa of the Conquest of {{ill|Mara (demon)|en|Mara (demon)|WD=Q1352021|lt=Mara|1=Mara (demon)}}", this stupa symbolizes the 35-year-old Buddha's attainment of enlightenment under the bodhi tree in {{ill|Bodh Gaya|en|Bodh Gaya|WD=Q176767|lt=Bodh Gaya|1=Bodh Gaya}}, where he conquered worldly temptations and attacks, manifesting in the form of Mara.<ref name="Beer"/>
===Stupa of Many Doors=== This stupa is also known as the "Stupa of Many Gates". After reaching enlightenment, the Buddha taught his first students in a deer park near {{ill|Sarnath|en|Sarnath|WD=Q324394|lt=Sarnath|1=Sarnath}}. The series of doors on each side of the steps represents the first teachings: the {{ill|Four Noble Truths|en|Four Noble Truths|WD=Q169010|lt=Four Noble Truths|1=Four Noble Truths}}, the Six {{ill|Pāramitā|en|Pāramitā|WD=Q828201|lt=Pāramitā|1=Pāramitā}}s, the {{ill|Noble Eightfold Path|en|Noble Eightfold Path|WD=Q185514|lt=Noble Eightfold Path|1=Noble Eightfold Path}}, and the {{ill|Twelve Nidānas|en|Twelve Nidānas|WD=Q249618|lt=Twelve Nidānas|1=Twelve Nidānas}}.<ref name="Beer"/>
===Stupa of Descent from the God Realm=== At 42 years of age, Buddha spent a summer retreat in the [[Tushita|Tuṣita Heaven]], where his mother had taken rebirth. In order to repay her kindness, he taught the dharma to her rebirth. Local inhabitants built a stupa in [[:en:Sankassa|Sankassa]] in order to commemorate this event. This type of stupa is characterized by having a central projection at each side, containing a triple ladder, or steps.<ref name="Beer"/>
===Stupa of Great Miracles=== Also known as the "Stupa of Conquest of the [[:en:Tirthika|Tirthika]]s", this stupa refers to various miracles performed by the Buddha when he was 50 years old. Legend claims that he overpowered ''maras'' and heretics by engaging them in intellectual arguments and also by performing miracles. This stupa was raised by the [[:en:Licchavi (kingdom)|Lichavi]] kingdom to commemorate the event.<ref name="Beer"/>
===Stupa of Reconciliation=== This stupa commemorates the Buddha's resolution of a dispute among the ''[[:en:Sangha (Buddhism)|sangha]]''. A stupa in this design was built in the kingdom of [[:en:Magadha (Mahajanapada)|Magadha]], where the reconciliation occurred. It has four octagonal steps with equal sides.<ref name="Beer"/>
===Stupa of Complete Victory=== This stupa commemorates Buddha's successful prolonging of his life by three months. It has only three steps, which are circular and unadorned.<ref name="Beer"/> {{Buddhism|collapsed=1}}
===Stupa of Nirvana=== This stupa refers to the ''{{ill|Parinirvana|en|Parinirvana|WD=Q375237|lt=Parinirvana|1=Parinirvana}}'', or death of the Buddha, when he was 80 years old. It symbolizes his complete absorption into the highest state of mind. It is bell-shaped and usually unornamented.<ref name="Beer"/>
==Kalachakra stupa== {{Main|Kalachakra stupa}}
A ninth kind of stupa exists, the {{ill|Kalachakra stupa|en|Kalachakra stupa|WD=Q1103381|lt=Kalachakra stupa|1=Kalachakra stupa}}. Its symbolism is not connected to events in the Buddha's life but instead to the symbolism of the [[:en:Kalachakra Tantra|Kalachakra Tantra]], created to protect against negative energies.<ref>{{cite web|title=Kalachakra Stupa |url=http://www.karmaguen.org/stupa_kalachakra_en.html |publisher=karmaguen.org |access-date=18 April 2009 |url-status = dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081205055317/http://www.karmaguen.org/stupa_kalachakra_en.html |archive-date=5 December 2008 }}</ref>
